strengths: Well-motivated interactive UI-to-code paradigm with clear practical justification based on rendering dependencies and visual feedback requirements
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple benchmarks (Design2Code, Flame, Web2Code) with two new proposed benchmarks (UI2Code-Real, UIPolish-bench)
Strong empirical results showing 35% average improvement over open-source baselines and competitive performance with closed-source models like Claude-4-Sonnet
Thorough ablation studies demonstrating VLM-based rewards significantly outperform CLIP-based alternatives for both UI polishing and UI-to-code tasks
Unified model handling three complementary capabilities (UI-to-code, UI polishing, UI editing) providing more versatility than prior single-task approaches
Clear, well-structured presentation with thoughtful treatment of data quality tradeoffs between real noisy webpages and clean synthetic data
weaknesses: Critical reproducibility issues: Training pipeline depends on proprietary models (Claude-3.7-Sonnet for SFT data, fine-tuned GLM-4.5V for RL rewards, o4-mini and Gemini-2.5-Pro for evaluation), preventing researchers without industry resources from reproducing the work

Evaluation methodology relies entirely on VLM-based metrics without human validation; uses different evaluators for different tasks (o4-mini vs. Gemini-2.5-Pro) with no sensitivity analysis of evaluator choice

Limited scientific novelty: interactive/iterative refinement is well-established; three-stage training is standard practice in VLM development; round-robin reward design is incremental rather than fundamental
Benchmark scale concerns: UI2Code-Real contains only 115 samples; UIPolish-bench size not clearly specified; both far smaller than standard ML benchmarks and insufficient for strong empirical claims

Missing critical comparisons: No empirical evaluation against acknowledged agent-based approaches (ScreenCoder, DECLARUI, DCGen) mentioned in related work; no systematic ablation of interactive vs. single-turn paradigm

Data quality concerns inadequately addressed: Claude-generated ground-truth HTML for SFT lacks quality validation; RL uses only 12K real webpages from navigation dataset (Mind2Web) with unclear transfer; no functional correctness evaluation of generated code
O(N²) VLM API calls in reward design (Algorithm 3) creates unfair reproducibility barrier and substantial computational/financial costs, limiting broader adoption
No human evaluation validation of VLM-based metrics; no error analysis or discussion of failure modes; practical applicability to functional correctness and code maintainability unclear

strengths: Practically motivated interactive paradigm that aligns with real UI development workflows
Thorough ablation studies on reward design (Section 4.3) with clear progression from baseline to comparator to round-robin approach
Comprehensive three-stage training pipeline (continual pre-training, SFT, RL) with thoughtful engineering choices
Strong empirical results on multiple benchmarks (Design2Code, Flame, Web2Code) compared to both open- and closed-source models
Attempts to address underexplored areas (UI polishing, UI editing) with new benchmark contributions
weaknesses: Critical circular dependency: GLM-4.5V used for both RL training rewards and primary evaluation metrics, creating systematic bias that cannot be separated from model quality
Small and inadequately validated benchmarks: UI2Code-Real (115 samples) and UIPolish-bench (200 samples) lack inter-annotator agreement and human validation procedures
Inconsistent results across benchmarks unexplained (beats GPT-5 on Flame but loses on Design2Code; relative performance varies dramatically), raising questions about benchmark validity
Limited technical novelty: applies standard techniques (continual pre-training, SFT, RL) to domain without algorithmic innovations; comparator function is incremental engineering
Flawed UI polishing evaluation metric: 'if C > B' only measures relative improvement, not absolute quality; both C and B could be poor

Incomplete reproducibility: training data not fully documented, closed-source VLM dependencies are stochastic, no error bars or confidence intervals across any results, missing computational cost analysis
Overclaimed results: claims performance 'comparable to GPT-5 and Claude-4-Sonnet' but Design2Code shows GPT-5 89.7 > UI2CodeN 88.6, inconsistent across benchmarks
No human evaluation, no failure analysis, missing limitations discussion; test-time scaling shows only modest gains (8% over 5 rounds) without cost-benefit analysis
Insufficient comparison with related work: references agent-based approaches but provides no quantitative comparisons; underexplores UI editing and polishing capabilities beyond qualitative examples
Data contamination risks not addressed: continual pre-training on Common Crawl overlaps with test benchmarks sourced from real websites; potential for test leakage not discussed

strengths: Well-motivated interactive UI-to-code paradigm that convincingly reframes code generation as iterative feedback-driven process, grounded in real developer workflows and technical necessity

Strong empirical results demonstrating SOTA among open-source models (88.6 Design2Code vs 64.7 for GLM-4.1V-9B) and competitive performance with closed-source systems; test-time scaling shows consistent 8-point improvement
Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple benchmarks, diverse baselines, and thorough ablation studies demonstrating VLM rewards outperform CLIP-based alternatives
Thoughtful technical execution with progressive reward design refinement (baseline → comparator → round-robin comparator) addressing calibration drift and fairness concerns
Contributes new benchmarks (UI2Code-Real, UIPolish-Bench) that address gaps in evaluating iterative refinement capabilities
Careful multi-stage training strategy that pragmatically balances scale (10M real data) with quality (80K curated SFT samples), supported by controlled ablations
weaknesses: Limited core methodological novelty: three-stage training pipeline (pretrain→SFT→RL) and GRPO with VLM rewards follow established practices; primary contribution is careful application rather than novel algorithms

Heavy reliance on VLM-based evaluation metrics (o4-mini, Gemini-2.5-Pro) with limited analysis of metric reliability; lack of correlation studies with actual code execution quality or functional metrics; 80-point threshold appears arbitrary

Significant reproducibility limitations: crawled 10M dataset not released; RL verification depends on proprietary GLM-4.5V model; code/models availability promised without concrete URL; researchers cannot easily replicate training pipeline

Insufficient error analysis: no systematic study of failure modes, hard UI patterns, or when polishing helps vs. hurts; missing qualitative failure cases and breakdown of improvement sources across polishing rounds

Benchmark scale concerns: UI2Code-Real (115 examples) and UIPolish-Bench (200 examples) are small; no confidence intervals or statistical significance testing reported; sampling strategy for real-world benchmarks not clearly described

Baseline fairness issues: strongest open-source baseline (GLM-4.1V) from same family as base model; closed-source comparisons may unfairly compare models not optimized for UI-to-code with UI2CodeN which is task-specialized

Missing practical analyses: no evaluation of inference latency for test-time scaling, production readiness metrics, functional code quality (responsiveness, accessibility), or code complexity; scope limited to web UI without evaluation on mobile/desktop paradigms

Limited dataset transparency: use of expensive Claude-3.7-Sonnet-Thinking for SFT data generation mentioned only in footnote; contribution of data generation cost vs. other components unclear; no inter-annotator agreement metrics for curated benchmarks

strengths: Novel problem formulation: Reconceptualizing UI-to-code as interactive visual optimization is well-motivated and compelling, addressing fundamental properties of UI coding that single-pass generation cannot handle
Principled technical approach: RVPO elegantly addresses non-differentiable visual objectives via relative ranking optimization, avoiding calibration issues of absolute rewards
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Multiple benchmarks, both VLM- and CLIP-based metrics, extensive human studies (Pearson 0.93 agreement), thorough ablations, and variance analysis across runs
Strong empirical results: 9B model achieves state-of-the-art or competitive performance with 5-10× larger models; consistent improvements with iterative refinement validate the core hypothesis
Excellent reproducibility: Detailed implementation specs, data collection procedures, ethical considerations, and commitment to open-source release support reproducibility
Honest limitations discussion: Addresses reward hacking (Table 6), convergence oscillations (Table 17), and evaluator sensitivity across multiple VLMs
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: RVPO is straightforward application of GRPO with tournament aggregation; three-stage training follows standard practices. Novelty resides in problem formulation, not methodology

Evaluation circularity: The model is optimized with RVPO rewards from a learned visual evaluator (fine-tuned GLM-4.5V), which then evaluates the model. Sample-level human-VLM correlation is only Pearson 0.65, and success threshold of 80 is arbitrary

Concerning convergence behavior: Polish success rate drops to 53.1% for high-quality cases (score ≥80), indicating the method may degrade outputs near convergence. Microscopic oscillations suggest instability despite macroscopic stability

Limited generalization scope: All evaluations are web-based UI tasks; no evaluation on mobile UIs, native apps, or other domains. Small benchmarks (UI2Code-Real: 115 samples, UIPolish-bench: 200 total)
Incomplete computational analysis: Training cost comparison missing; rendering and pairwise comparison overhead during RL not fully analyzed. No FLOPS comparison with baseline VLM training

Inadequate failure mode analysis: Minimal discussion of when/why method fails; 25-48% error rates on some benchmarks unexplained. No characterization of visual attributes or structures most challenging for the approach

Incomplete ablations: No systematic study of refinement iterations vs test-time cost tradeoff. Unclear how much improvement comes from RVPO specifically vs RL with absolute VLM rewards. Limited analysis of group size impact in tournament aggregation
Reward hacking concerns: Only checks for hard-coded positioning; multi-aspect evaluation doesn't guarantee safety against all shortcuts. Limited discussion of robustness to distribution shifts
Qualitative understanding gap: What specific error types does RL fix vs SFT? Demo cases are mostly qualitative; quantitative analysis of improvement types missing

strengths: Well-motivated problem reformulation: Compelling argument that UI development is inherently iterative, providing better alignment with real-world workflows than single-pass generation

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Extensive benchmarking across multiple datasets (Design2Code, Flame, Web2Code, UI2Code-Real, UIPolish-bench) with human studies, evaluator validation, variance analysis, and ablations
Strong empirical results: Achieves competitive performance with much smaller model (9B vs 32B-78B) and demonstrates test-time scaling via iterative refinement
Careful evaluation methodology: Human-VLM alignment studies (Pearson 0.93, Spearman 1.0), multi-judge consistency analysis, and structured variance testing demonstrate research rigor
Well-engineered three-stage training pipeline: Complementary contributions from continual pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning are clearly demonstrated through ablations
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: RVPO is largely Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO, Shao et al. 2024) with straightforward tournament-based reward construction. The 'Visual' qualifier reflects application domain rather than algorithmic innovation, and the core objective (Eq. 7) is standard preference-based RL

Inconsistent and problematic evaluation methodology: Different evaluators used for different tasks (o4-mini vs Gemini-2.5-Pro), justified post-hoc; arbitrary accuracy threshold (score ≥ 80) without sensitivity analysis; human evaluation limited to 80-100 samples; main results lack confidence intervals
Small and potentially non-representative benchmarks: UI2Code-Real has only 115 samples; UIPolish benchmark variants have 100 samples each—insufficient for robust generalization claims

Incomplete analysis of interactive optimization benefits: Test-time scaling plateaus quickly (Table 3); no computational cost analysis; missing guidance on practical stopping criteria; no comparison with simpler iterative baselines

Confounded improvements and incomplete ablations: Section 4.3 compares only to single 'absolute verifier' baseline; unclear whether gains come from relative preferences, RL formulation, specific reward design, or training data quantity; no comparison with other preference-based RL methods (DPO, IPO)

Weak baseline comparisons: Mostly against general-purpose VLMs rather than UI-to-code specialists; specialized models relegated to Appendix Table 14; inconsistent metrics across comparisons (DINO vs VLM scores); modest RL gain (+9.3% in Table 11) relative to pipeline complexity
Inadequate treatment of UI Editing: Only human study on 69 samples (Table 4); significant restriction to 'localized, well-specified changes' barely discussed; underdeveloped as a core contribution

Unsubstantiated data quality claims: Training data construction vague (12K 'real-world' examples from Mind2Web); no overlap analysis between training and test; hash-based deduplication may miss semantic near-duplicates

Domain and generalization limitations: Evaluation exclusively on HTML/CSS; no evidence for claimed 'model-agnostic' applicability; no failure mode analysis or error categorization; unclear generalization to mobile, desktop, or other platforms

strengths: Novel problem formulation: Reframing UI-to-code as interactive visual optimization is genuinely well-motivated and original, with clear justification from properties of real-world UI development
Sound technical approach: RVPO's tournament-based reward aggregation is a principled solution to handle non-differentiable visual objectives and noisy VLM evaluators

Comprehensive experimental validation: Multiple benchmarks (Design2Code, Flame, Web2Code, custom UI2Code-Real, UIPolish-Bench), evaluation paradigms (CLIP, VLM, human), extensive ablations, and strong human-VLM alignment (Pearson r=0.93)
Strong empirical results: Achieves competitive or superior performance to significantly larger closed-source models with only 9B parameters; demonstrates consistent test-time scaling improvements
Reproducibility and ethics: Detailed training procedures with hyperparameters, comprehensive ethics statement, PII protection measures, and promised open-source release
Thorough ablation studies: Reward design impact, training stages, real-world data effects, evaluator sensitivity across 4 different VLMs, and variance stability across 5 runs
weaknesses: Evaluation methodology circularity: Model trained with VLM-based rewards then evaluated with similar VLM judges, creating potential bias; human evaluation limited to 80 samples with 2 annotators for Design2Code-HARD
Generalization limitations: UI2Code-Real contains only 115 examples; no evaluation on mobile UIs, progressive web apps, or paradigms beyond desktop HTML/CSS; all demo cases lack edge case analysis

Technical clarity gaps: The implicit visual distance D (Eq. 2) remains undefined; connection between rank-based surrogate (Eq. 7) and tournament approximation loses theoretical grounding; RVPO is essentially GRPO with tournament aggregation but positioned as major contribution

Polishing process instability: Polish success rate drops from 74.5% (low-quality) to 53.1% (high-quality cases); individual-sample oscillations dismissed without rigorous analysis; different saturation points between synthetic and real data unexplained
Incomplete reward hacking analysis: Only measures absolute positioning ratio; doesn't analyze other shortcuts or functional correctness vs. visual fidelity trade-offs

Computational efficiency under-analyzed: Inference latency not broken down (token generation vs. rendering); training costs (GPU-hours, memory) not discussed; multiple renders during refinement cost not fully assessed
Arbitrary design choices: 80-point success threshold (Eq. 19) lacks justification or sensitivity analysis; different evaluators for drafting vs. polishing without justification for this choice
